newsitem.title: CANADA: UAL sees strong demand for Pacific freight.
newsitem.headline: UAL sees strong demand for Pacific freight.

text.p: Initial customer response to United Airlines' Pacific freighter service which begins March 3 is exceeding expectations, causing the airline to ponder adding aircraft and routes, says cargo vice-president Jim Hartigan.
Expansion beyond the first four aircraft would continue to focus on U.S.-Asia corridors, he said from Chicago.
"The reception has been nothing short of tremendous," said Hartigan. "We're very, very, very pleased with the reaction of the marketplace."
The initial flights will all go out fairly full in both directions, he said.

"Overall, the total net revenue is actually stronger than the forecast we made about 14 months ago. And if you believe what you see on paper, eastbound and westbound revenue are going to shake out pretty close to each other," in part because of strong U.S.-to-Manila traffic and yields.

Hartigan wouldn't disclose when the service will be profitable, but said advance bookings suggest the freighters are on track to meet the profit targets set for them over a year ago when the proposal for a freighter service was pitched to the board of UAL Corp.
Conversion of the first of four DC-10-30F aircraft is complete, with delivery to United set for Wednesday.
That aircraft will launch a Chicago-Anchorage Osaka-Manila service on March 3, said Hartigan.

The second aircraft is due for delivery March 6, and will be put into service March 17 on a Chicago-Los Angeles-Anchorage-Osaka routing, with continuing service to either Taipei or Manila, depending on the day.
Later in the year, that Los Angeles stop will be dropped after the third and fourth aircraft are converted. They leave passenger service in April for conversion in Italy.
No later than Sept 15, one will be put into service on a Chicago-New York-Anchorage-Tokyo routing, while the other will fly LA-San Francisco-Anchorage-Osaka, continuing to Taipei or Manila.

The aircraft have a rated capacity of 68 tons, but usually will carry 60-63 tons. Schedules are being coordinated so the aircraft are on the ground in Anchorage at the same time, allowing United to sell any of the four Asian destinations from any of the five US gateways and vice-versa.
So far, traffic and yields to/from Chicago and Manila are stronger than forecast, said Hartigan. To and from the US West Coast, traffic is a bit stronger than forecast, but yields a bit softer.
Even with abundant freighter competition to Osaka from the likes of UPS and Nippon Cargo Airlines, Hartigan says United has been "very successful" in gaining commitments for Osaka space.

United's initial emphasis on Osaka - as opposed to focussing exclusively on Tokyo where it operates a major passenger hub - stems from an expectation Japanese authorities will cap 1998 Osaka frequencies for all carriers at summer 1997 levels because of a developing shortage of runway capacity, said Hartigan.
"I have to protect my slots at Osaka so that's why we're starting there first," he said.
